neighbors.heading: overcome evil by good
neighbors.text: Today an old verse said hatred never ends by hatred, only by love. Catholics hear Jesus say something close on a mountainside: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." Paul adds a short rule of his own: "Be not overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good."
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada calls this an old law, simply how hatred works, like fire. For Catholics, loving an enemy imitates God the Father, who sends rain on the just and the unjust, and it is made possible by grace.
neighbors.shared: hatred stops where someone refuses to pass it on.

neighbors.heading: no one is my enemy
neighbors.text: Today an old verse said hatred ends only by love. Sikhs sing something close. Guru Arjan wrote that since he found the company of the holy, no one is his enemy and no one a stranger; he gets along with all. And Baba Farid, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, says: answer evil with good, and don't let anger fill your mind.
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada roots this in how the mind works. For Sikhs, no one is finally an enemy because the one God's light shines in every person.
neighbors.shared: anger set down is lighter than anger carried.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Salok Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not in our hands
neighbors.text: Today Job's friends explained his suffering, and the book says they were wrong. Jewish sages kept that humility. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Yannai says, in paraphrase: it is not in our hands to explain why the wicked are at ease or why the righteous suffer. And when a sick rabbi was asked if his sufferings were dear to him, he said: neither they nor their reward.
neighbors.difference: Job is a story where God himself rebukes the explainers. The rabbis kept more than one voice: some did look for reasons, even calling some pain "sufferings of love", and the Talmud sets those beside the humbler answer.
neighbors.shared: not every pain needs an explanation; sometimes it needs a hand.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 4:15 (4:19 in some editions) (paraphrase) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 5a-5b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not all from past deeds
neighbors.text: Today Job's friends insisted his suffering must be deserved. A man named Sivaka once asked the Buddha something close: is everything we feel caused by past deeds? No, the Buddha said, in paraphrase. Some pain comes from the body, some from the change of seasons, from carelessness, from violence done to us, and some from past action. To say it's all past deeds goes too far.
neighbors.difference: Job's question is about a just God and an innocent man. The Buddha speaks of no God who judges; karma is real for him, just not the whole explanation of every pain.
neighbors.shared: not every wound is a verdict on the one who carries it.

neighbors.heading: this is mercy
neighbors.text: Today Jesus wept at his friend's tomb, and the people said, see how he loved him. Muslims remember a father's tears too. When the Prophet's ﷺ baby son Ibrahim was dying, his eyes filled, and a companion was surprised. The Prophet said, in paraphrase: this is mercy. The eyes weep and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, Jesus is the Son of God made flesh, so these are God's own tears. For Muslims, Muhammad ﷺ is a human messenger, not divine, and his tears show the mercy God places in human hearts.
neighbors.shared: tears for someone you love are not a lack of faith.

neighbors.heading: Rama weeps in the forest
neighbors.text: Today Jesus wept for Lazarus, and his tears showed his love. Hindus tell of tears like that in the Ramayana. When Sita is taken, Rama searches the forest weeping, asking the trees, the rivers and the deer whether they have seen her. Many Hindus honor Rama as an avatar of Vishnu, and the epic doesn't hide his grief.
neighbors.difference: Christians speak of one incarnation, Jesus, who weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb. Hindus speak of Vishnu coming down in many forms; some read Rama's grief as fully human, others as divine play.
neighbors.shared: grief is how love looks when someone is missing.

neighbors.heading: a bow made of patience
neighbors.text: Today Jacob lost his son and chose a beautiful patience, sabr. The same word lives in the Sikh scripture. Baba Farid, whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, says, in paraphrase: let patience be your bow, patience your bowstring, patience your arrow, and the Creator will not let it miss.
neighbors.difference: In the Quran, Jacob is a prophet whose patience carries his grief to God, and the story gives Joseph back. Farid's patience aims at God himself: its hope is nearness to the Creator.
neighbors.shared: patience isn't giving up; it's holding steady while you hope.

neighbors.heading: patient in tribulation
neighbors.text: Today Jacob grieved for Joseph with a beautiful patience. Christians know the same father from Genesis, where his children try to comfort him, "but he refused to be comforted." And Paul, writing to Christians in Rome, asks for a patience that still hopes: "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer."
neighbors.difference: In the Quran, Jacob names his patience beautiful and takes his grief to God alone. In Genesis, he refuses comfort outright, and Christians hear Paul's patience as hope fixed on Christ.
neighbors.shared: you can grieve hard and still keep a door open to hope.

neighbors.heading: self is the lord of self
neighbors.text: Today Frankl said one freedom stays when everything else is taken: the stance you choose. An old Buddhist verse points to the same inner ground: "Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?" Many Buddhists train it in small ways, noticing anger or fear as it rises and letting it pass before it acts.
neighbors.difference: Frankl found meaning by choosing a stance toward suffering. Buddhist practice aims at seeing through the craving behind suffering, and it also teaches that no fixed, lasting self lies underneath.
neighbors.shared: what happens to you isn't all that happens in you.

neighbors.heading: a martyr of charity
neighbors.text: Today Frankl said one freedom can't be taken: how you meet what happens. Catholics remember a priest who used that freedom in Auschwitz. Maximilian Kolbe, a Franciscan prisoner, stepped forward to die in place of a man condemned to starve, a husband and father. The Church reads his choice by Jesus' words: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends."
neighbors.difference: Frankl, a psychiatrist, writes of a freedom every person has, whatever they believe. Catholics see Kolbe's choice as grace: Christ's own love at work in him, given for someone else.
neighbors.shared: even with almost everything taken, love can still choose.
neighbors.sources: John 15:13 (Douay-Rheims) · St. Maximilian Kolbe, honored by the Church as a martyr of charity (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: their pain as your own
neighbors.text: Today's practice said: this is hard, and others feel this too. The Bhagavad Gita turns that thought outward. Krishna says, in paraphrase, that the highest yogi is the one who, by the likeness of their own self, sees the joy and the pain of every being as their own. Your own hurt becomes a window onto everyone's.
neighbors.difference: Neff's practice is kindness turned inward, grounded in psychology. In the Gita the likeness runs deeper: Krishna teaches seeing the Self in every being, so another's pain truly concerns you.
neighbors.shared: you're not the only one who hurts, and neither are they.

neighbors.heading: you know the heart of a stranger
neighbors.text: Today's practice said: this is hard, and others feel this too. The Torah builds a law on that same knowing: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." Remembered pain, the verse says, is how you understand someone else's.
neighbors.difference: Neff's common humanity is something you remind yourself of, to be kinder to yourself. The Torah makes it a commandment, rooted in a whole people's memory of Egypt, and points it at the stranger.
neighbors.shared: your own hard days can make you gentler with everyone else's.

neighbors.heading: by whose stripes
neighbors.text: Today an old myth said a healer's own wound can help them understand. Christians say something like it about Jesus himself. A letter to the Hebrews says: "For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted." And Peter's letter speaks of Christ, "by whose stripes ye were healed."
neighbors.difference: In the myth and in modern care, a hurt person helps others by understanding them. Christians believe Christ's wounds do more than understand: they heal and save, as God's own self-giving.
neighbors.shared: the ones who've been hurt often know best how to sit with hurt.

neighbors.heading: once an orphan
neighbors.text: Today an old myth said a healer's own wound can help them heal others. The Quran speaks to the Prophet ﷺ in that spirit. It reminds him, in paraphrase: did God not find you an orphan and give you shelter? Did He not find you in need and provide? So do not be harsh with the orphan, and do not turn away the one who asks.
neighbors.difference: The wounded-healer idea says hurt can deepen understanding. The Quran ties it to gratitude to God: you were sheltered, so shelter others, as a command, not only a gift of empathy.
neighbors.shared: what was once done for you can become what you do for others.

neighbors.heading: sow in tears
neighbors.text: Today Seneca looked at a burned city and said it could rise again. Catholics pray a psalm about a people coming home from ruin: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." And the Easter Vigil begins in darkness: a new fire is lit, and its light is carried into the dark church.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's hope rests on nature's cycles and a steady mind: what falls can be rebuilt. For Catholics, hope rests on God, who raised Christ from the tomb and can bring life out of ruin.
neighbors.shared: ruin is real, and so is rebuilding.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 125:5 (Douay-Rheims; Psalm 126:5 in many Bibles) · the Easter Vigil (described)

neighbors.heading: chardi kala
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said a burned city can rise again. Sikhs have a word for a spirit that keeps rising: chardi kala. Their daily prayer, the Ardas, remembers Sikhs who suffered terribly for their faith, and still it closes: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. With the Name, spirits rise; in your will, may all be well.
neighbors.difference: Seneca steadies himself with reason: expect loss, then rebuild. For Sikhs, chardi kala isn't only a strong mind; it's kept by remembering God's Name and accepting God's will.
neighbors.shared: a spirit can stay high even while the walls are down.
neighbors.sources: Ardas, the Sikh daily prayer (paraphrase of the closing line)

neighbors.heading: plant the sapling first
neighbors.text: Today Montaigne hoped death would find him planting cabbages. A Jewish sage, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, gave planting its place even at the end of days. In paraphrase: if you are holding a sapling and someone cries that the Messiah has come, plant the sapling first, then go out to greet him.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne wants to meet his own death unbothered, busy with ordinary work. The rabbi's saying looks to the world's future and God's promise: even then, the work in your hands still matters.
neighbors.shared: keep planting; the ordinary work of today is never wasted.

neighbors.heading: today the effort
neighbors.text: Today Montaigne said that to philosophize is to learn to die. A Buddhist verse, the teaching of One Fine Night, says it in its own way, in paraphrase: don't chase the past or pine for the future; see clearly what is here now. Do today what needs doing. Who knows? Death may come tomorrow.
neighbors.difference: Montaigne wants death to be familiar so it stops ruling him. In the Buddha's verse, remembering death fuels the effort to see clearly and, in time, to be free of the round of rebirth.
neighbors.shared: today is the one day you can be sure of.

neighbors.heading: as a traveler
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha praised the monk who remembers death within a single breath. Muslims keep a saying close to that. The Prophet ﷺ told Ibn Umar, in paraphrase: be in this world as a stranger or a traveler. And Ibn Umar would add: in the evening, don't count on morning; in the morning, don't count on evening. Take from your health for your sickness.
neighbors.difference: For the Buddha, remembering death sharpens practice toward the deathless. For Muslims, it is preparation to meet God, who will weigh each life, with hope in God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: an honest look at the end makes this hour count.

neighbors.heading: what you remember at the end
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked his monks to remember death with every breath. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, in paraphrase: whatever a person remembers as they leave the body, to that they go. So remember me at all times, and do your duty. The last moment is shaped by all the ordinary ones before it.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's monks remember death to stay awake and reach the deathless, teaching no lasting self that passes on. In the Gita, the self goes on, and remembering Krishna carries it to him.
neighbors.shared: how we spend ordinary moments shapes the last one.

neighbors.heading: sing, don't weep
neighbors.text: Today the mourner's Kaddish praised God and never named death. Sikhs keep something close. A poem in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sadd, remembers Guru Amar Das asking, near his end, that no one weep for him, but that they sing God's praise and hear God's word instead. Sikh funerals often include kirtan, hymns sung to the one who gave life.
neighbors.difference: The Kaddish keeps tears and praise together, said by mourners in a gathered quorum. Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul going home to God, and the Guru asks that the praise come without weeping.
neighbors.shared: praise can still be sung with a broken heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Ramkali, Sadd (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: blessed be the name
neighbors.text: Today the Kaddish praised God beside a grave. In the old Anglican prayer book, Christians walk to the grave praising too. The burial service opens with sentences from Scripture, among them Job's: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the Name of the Lord." Grief and praise walk in together.
neighbors.difference: The mourner's Kaddish never mentions death. The Christian service names it plainly, and its first words are Jesus' own, "I am the resurrection and the life", so its praise leans on the hope of rising in Christ.
neighbors.shared: praising God at a grave is faith said out loud.
neighbors.sources: Book of Common Prayer 1662, The Order for the Burial of the Dead · Job 1:21 · John 11:25

neighbors.heading: Ananda at the door
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son and called the tears mercy. Buddhists remember tears near the end of the Buddha's life. His attendant Ananda went inside, leaned on the doorpost and wept. The Buddha called him and said, in paraphrase: enough, Ananda, don't grieve. Haven't I told you that all we hold dear must change? Then he praised Ananda's years of loving care.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, tears are called mercy, held within what pleases God. The Buddha comforts Ananda by pointing to impermanence, a truth to see through, so that grief can loosen its grip.
neighbors.shared: even the closest followers wept, and were met with tenderness.

neighbors.heading: a sword through her soul
neighbors.text: Today the Prophet ﷺ wept for his son and called the tears mercy. Catholics keep a mother's grief close. When Mary brought her baby to the Temple, Simeon told her: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." An old hymn, the Stabat Mater, pictures her at the cross, weeping, close to her Son to the last. Catholics honor her as Our Lady of Sorrows.
neighbors.difference: In the hadith, a prophet weeps as a father and says only what pleases God. Catholics see Mary's sorrow joined to her Son's suffering for the world, and many ask her prayers in their own grief.
neighbors.shared: a parent's grief is love with nowhere left to go.

neighbors.heading: rice and water for the ancestors
neighbors.text: Today families swept their ancestors' tombs at Qingming. Hindu families keep a season for this too: Pitru Paksha, the fortnight of the ancestors. In shraddha rites they offer pinda, balls of rice, with water and sesame, and speak the names of parents and grandparents. An old Upanishad tells students leaving their teacher: do not neglect your duties to the gods and to the ancestors.
neighbors.difference: At Qingming, care is shown at the grave itself. Hindus usually cremate, so there's no grave to sweep; shraddha offerings, believed to nourish the ancestors, are made at home or beside a holy river.
neighbors.shared: the people who came before you are still worth tending.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (paraphrase) · shraddha and Pitru Paksha customs (described)

neighbors.heading: a candle for the year's turn
neighbors.text: Today families swept their ancestors' tombs. Jewish families keep a day too: the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death. A candle burns through the day, and Kaddish is said. Many link the flame to a proverb: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." At the grave, visitors often leave a small stone to show someone came.
neighbors.difference: At Qingming, many families set out food and paper offerings the dead might need. Jewish practice offers nothing to the dead; the living pray to God, give charity and study in their memory.
neighbors.shared: remembering is done with hands: a stone, a flame, a cleared grave.

neighbors.heading: rich toward God
neighbors.text: Today a hospice nurse said the dying often wish they hadn't worked so hard. Jesus told a story about that. A rich man plans bigger barns and a long, easy rest. Then God says: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?"
neighbors.difference: Ware's regrets are about living true to yourself and the people you love. Jesus' story points past that, to being "rich toward God": a life measured by God, not only by your own heart.
neighbors.shared: the end shows what mattered; it's kinder to look now.

neighbors.heading: until ye come to the graves
neighbors.text: Today a hospice nurse heard the dying wish they had lived less for other people's expectations. A short chapter of the Quran says it in two lines: "Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you until ye come to the graves." Another verse pictures someone at death asking, in paraphrase: Lord, give me a little more time, and I would give in charity and do good.
neighbors.difference: Ware's regrets look back over a life, measured by its own truest wishes. The Quran adds an accounting before God, and asks for the change now, while there's still time to give.
neighbors.shared: you don't have to wait for the end to see what matters.

neighbors.heading: the communion of saints
neighbors.text: Today grief researchers said many people keep a bond with those who've died. Catholics say that bond is real. In the Creed they profess "the communion of saints": the living and the dead, one family in Christ. They pray for their dead by name, and an old book says: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead."
neighbors.difference: Researchers describe the bond as memory and meaning carried by the mourner, without saying where the dead are. Catholics believe the dead live in God, and that prayer truly reaches and helps them.
neighbors.shared: love doesn't have to end where a life does.
neighbors.sources: Apostles' Creed · 2 Machabees 12:46 (Douay-Rheims; 2 Maccabees in many Bibles)

neighbors.heading: named in every Ardas
neighbors.text: Today grief researchers said keeping a bond with the dead can be healthy. Sikhs remember their dead aloud. The Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, names the Gurus and recalls the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith. When someone dies, families often hold a reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, with a prayer that the soul rest at God's feet.
neighbors.difference: Researchers speak of a bond kept inside the mourner. Sikh teaching sees the soul returning to God, and the Gurus turned away from rites meant to feed or serve the dead; remembrance is praise, not offering.
neighbors.shared: the ones we've lost can still be named with love.
neighbors.sources: Ardas, the Sikh prayer (described) · Sahaj Path and Ardas at a Sikh funeral (described)

neighbors.heading: pursue peace
neighbors.text: Today the texts said make peace before the sun goes down. Hillel put it as a calling: be like the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. The rabbis told how Aaron did it. When two people quarreled, he would sit with each one and say, the other is heartbroken over this, until they met and embraced.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's texts ask you to mend your own quarrels. Aaron, in the rabbis' telling, went further: he chased peace between other people, even, in that telling, shading the truth a little.
neighbors.shared: peace usually needs someone to go first.
neighbors.sources: Pirkei Avot 1:12 (paraphrase) · Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, 12 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: their quarrels cease
neighbors.text: Today the texts said make peace before the sun goes down. An old Buddhist verse gives its own reason: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here; but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." Remember the ending, the verse says, and the fight shrinks.
neighbors.difference: The lesson's texts ask for mending before God and the community. The Dhammapada speaks of no God here; quarrels end because death, seen clearly, makes them look small.
neighbors.shared: life is short enough that most quarrels aren't worth keeping.

neighbors.heading: your body has a right
neighbors.text: Today's lesson thanked the body that carried you here. Muslims remember a word from the Prophet ﷺ about this. When a young companion fasted every day and prayed all night, the Prophet told him, in paraphrase: fast some days and eat on others; pray, and sleep too. Your body has a right over you, and your eyes have a right over you.
neighbors.difference: The psalm praises the body as wonderfully made. Islam also frames it as a trust from God with rights of its own, so resting, eating and caring for it can be part of worship.
neighbors.shared: caring for your body is a kind of thank-you.

neighbors.heading: the first tool of dharma
neighbors.text: Today's lesson thanked the body that carried you here. A line from the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa is still quoted in Hindu homes: the body is the very first means of living dharma. In his poem, it's said to the goddess Parvati as she wears herself out with hard austerities: take care, the body is what makes the practice possible.
neighbors.difference: The psalm and the blessing thank God for a body that is made and fragile. Many Hindus see the body as a vehicle for the self, which is not the body: honored as the chariot, not the rider.
neighbors.shared: the body you have is the one that carries your practice.

neighbors.heading: the true company
neighbors.text: Today Aristotle said the best friends are good, and wish each other good. Sikhs prize that kind of company: the sangat. Guru Nanak asks, in paraphrase, how is the true company known? It's where the one Name is spoken. Sikhs gather in it to sing, serve and eat together, and the company itself helps make them good.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle's best friendships are rare, between people already good and alike. The sangat is open to anyone who comes, and gathers around God's Name rather than around two people.
neighbors.shared: the people you sit with help shape who you become.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: provoke unto love
neighbors.text: Today Aristotle said the best friends wish each other good for the other's own sake. An early Christian letter asks a whole church for that: "And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works." And Jesus tells his disciples: "I have called you friends."
neighbors.difference: Aristotle saves the highest friendship for a few equals in goodness. Christians call fellow believers, even strangers, brothers and sisters, and see their deepest friendship as one Christ offers first.
neighbors.shared: a good friend makes you want to be good.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today Ruth refused to leave Naomi: where you die, I will die. Buddhists honor faithful friendship too. Ananda once said good friends are half of the spiritual life. Not half, the Buddha answered, in paraphrase: good friendship is the whole of it. Elsewhere he says a true friend doesn't abandon you when you fall on hard times.
neighbors.difference: Ruth binds herself for life to Naomi's people and God. The Buddha's good friend is a companion on the path toward freedom, and Buddhists also teach not to cling, even to those dearest.
neighbors.shared: staying with someone through the hard years is a kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (paraphrase) · Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: behold thy mother
neighbors.text: Today Ruth chose Naomi: thy people shall be my people. Catholics keep a scene like it at the cross. Jesus, dying, sees his mother and the disciple he loved, and joins them: "Woman, behold thy son." Then: "Behold thy mother." And from that hour, the disciple "took her to his own."
neighbors.difference: Ruth chooses Naomi herself, at a cost to her own future. In John, Jesus gives the two to each other, and Catholics read it as Mary given as mother to every disciple.
neighbors.shared: family can be chosen, and kept, in the hardest hour.

neighbors.heading: a leaf, a flower
neighbors.text: Today Thérèse offered small things with great love, like strewing flowers. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says something close, in paraphrase: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, I accept it, offered from a devoted heart. In many Hindu homes, the daily offering is just that small.
neighbors.difference: Thérèse offers her small acts to Jesus, trusting his arms to lift her. Krishna speaks as the Lord receiving the gift himself; in bhakti, the love behind the offering is what reaches him.
neighbors.shared: nothing is too small when it's given with love.

neighbors.heading: much or little
neighbors.text: Today Thérèse said small acts of love count. The Talmud has a short line Jews still quote, in paraphrase: one may do much or one may do little, as long as the heart is turned toward Heaven. And Pirkei Avot asks for the same care with a light commandment as with a weighty one, since we can't know their reward.
neighbors.difference: Thérèse's little way is love offered to Jesus and lifted by grace. Jewish teaching ties the small deed to the mitzvot, the commandments, done faithfully for God, whose weight only God knows.
neighbors.shared: a small thing done with your whole heart is not small.

neighbors.heading: as a hen gathereth
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha asked for love as fierce as a mother's for her only child, spread to all beings. Jesus reaches for a mother's picture too. Grieving over a city that turned him away, he says: "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings."
neighbors.difference: In the Metta Sutta, a person grows boundless love step by step, without speaking of God. Jesus speaks of his own love, and Christians see in it God's love reaching out, even to those who turn away.
neighbors.shared: the fiercest love we know points to a wider one.

neighbors.heading: more merciful than a mother
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha pictured a mother guarding her only child. The Prophet ﷺ once pointed to a mother too. Among captives, a woman searched desperately, found her baby and held it to nurse. The Prophet asked, in paraphrase: would she ever throw her child into a fire? No, they said. God is more merciful to His servants than she is to her child.
neighbors.difference: The Metta Sutta asks people to grow a mother's love toward all beings. The hadith speaks of God's own mercy, greater than any mother's; Muslims see human mercy as a small share of it.
neighbors.shared: a mother's love is the closest picture we have of something bigger.

neighbors.heading: a lotus in the water
neighbors.text: Today equanimity meant loving without clinging. Sikhs have a picture for it. In the Sidh Gosht, a conversation with yogis, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: the lotus lives in the water and stays untouched; the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Live in the world like that, with your mind fixed on the Word.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist equanimity rests on seeing that beings own their deeds. Guru Nanak's loose grip comes from holding on to God's Name instead, and he asks for it inside family life, not apart from it.
neighbors.shared: you can hold people close without holding on too tight.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Raag Ramkali, Sidh Gosht (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: holy indifference
neighbors.text: Today equanimity meant an even heart, close enough to love, loose enough not to grab. Catholics in the Jesuit tradition call something like it indifference. St. Ignatius writes, in paraphrase: don't prefer health to sickness, riches to poverty, honor to dishonor, a long life to a short one; want only what best leads to the end we're made for, God.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist equanimity steadies love toward all beings, seeing that each owns their deeds. Ignatian indifference loosens the grip on everything so the heart is free to choose God; it isn't coldness toward people.
neighbors.shared: a loose grip can make room for a bigger love.
neighbors.sources: St. Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Principle and Foundation (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: betrothed every morning
neighbors.text: Today love was a daily choice, not only a feeling. On weekday mornings, Jews who wind tefillin around a finger say a vow from Hosea, God speaking to Israel like a groom: "I will betroth thee unto Me in righteousness, and in justice, and in lovingkindness, and in compassion." The same promise, renewed each morning.
neighbors.difference: Fromm and Paul describe love between people as an art practiced daily. Hosea's betrothal is God's covenant with a people; the morning vow binds a person to God, and couples can borrow its shape.
neighbors.shared: love gets chosen again, morning by morning.

neighbors.heading: in this life and the next
neighbors.text: Today love was a daily choice. The Buddha once met an old couple, Nakula's father and mother. The husband said, in paraphrase: since she came to me as a girl, I've never been unfaithful to her, even in thought. Both hoped to be together in lives to come. The Buddha said: if you match in faith, goodness, generosity and wisdom, you will.
neighbors.difference: Fromm treats love as an art of living for this life. In the Buddha's answer, a couple's shared goodness can carry their bond into lives to come, through karma and rebirth.
neighbors.shared: love lasts when it's grown together, day after day.

neighbors.heading: the wing of mercy
neighbors.text: Today honor meant actions, with honest limits. The Quran asks for both. In paraphrase: be kind to your parents; when they grow old, don't even sigh at them in irritation, and lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy. But if they press you to worship anything beside God, don't obey that, and still keep them company kindly in this world.
neighbors.difference: Exodus and the rabbis spell honor out as deeds. The Quran sets kindness to parents right beside worshipping God alone, and names its one limit plainly: no obeying them against God.
neighbors.shared: you can honor a parent and still keep your own conscience.

neighbors.heading: let your mother be a god to you
neighbors.text: Today honor meant care and respect, even when it's hard. An old Upanishad tells students leaving their teacher: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you. And Hindus tell of young Prahlada, who stayed respectful to his father, a cruel king, yet would not give up his love for Vishnu.
neighbors.difference: Exodus asks for honor, and Confucius for respect. The Upanishad asks that parents be treated as divine, while Prahlada's story shows even that honor stops short of turning from God.
neighbors.shared: honoring parents doesn't mean pretending they're perfect.
neighbors.sources: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 (paraphrase) · Bhagavata Purana, book 7, Prahlada (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seva
neighbors.text: Today drops of water filled a pot, a little at a time. Sikhs live this in seva, selfless service. At the gurdwara, people wipe shoes, wash dishes and roll rotis for the langar, the free kitchen where anyone can eat. Guru Arjan wrote, in paraphrase, that one who serves without wanting anything back reaches the Lord.
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada gathers good drop by drop toward a purer mind. Seva is offered to God through serving people, done side by side in a shared kitchen, without counting.
neighbors.shared: a plate washed for a stranger still counts.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (paraphrase) · langar and seva (described)

neighbors.heading: two mites
neighbors.text: Today small kindnesses added up like drops in a pot. Jesus once watched people giving at the Temple. Rich people gave much. "And there came a certain poor widow, and she threw in two mites." He tells his friends: "this poor widow hath cast more in, than all they which have cast into the treasury."
neighbors.difference: The Dhammapada counts small goods adding up over time. Jesus measures the widow by what it cost her, all she had, given to God, not by the size of the coin.
neighbors.shared: a gift is measured by the heart, not the amount.

neighbors.heading: a blessed thread
neighbors.text: Today a sister tied a rakhi, a thread of protection, on her brother's wrist. In Sri Lanka, Thailand and other Theravada Buddhist lands, monks chant protective verses called paritta while holding a white cotton thread. Afterward, pieces of the thread are tied around people's wrists, a reminder of the blessing and the teaching it carried.
neighbors.difference: A rakhi binds two people: a sister's prayer and a brother's promise. The paritta thread carries the blessing of chanted teachings, and Buddhist teachers say its real protection is a mind shaped by those words.
neighbors.shared: a light thread on the wrist can carry a heavy promise.
neighbors.sources: paritta chanting and the blessed thread (described) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8, often among the verses chanted

neighbors.heading: worn close
neighbors.text: Today a thin thread on a wrist carried a promise of protection. Some Catholics wear something small too: a scapular, two little squares of brown cloth on cords, or a blessed medal, as a sign of belonging to Mary and trusting her care. The Church calls these sacramentals: blessed signs that dispose a person to receive God's grace.
neighbors.difference: A rakhi is a bond between siblings, a brother pledging to stand by his sister. A scapular binds the wearer to Mary and to God, and the Church teaches it is no charm; it means something only with faith and prayer.
neighbors.shared: a small thing worn close can remind you you're not alone.
